planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in filtered shade; golden camellia is a frost-tender understory species best grown outdoors only in mild subtropical climates or under glass elsewhere.

directions: Golden camellia is one of a small group of wild yellow-flowered camellia species native to the limestone forest understory of Guangxi, China and adjacent northern Vietnam, prized by collectors because true yellow pigment is otherwise almost unknown in the genus. Waxy, nodding, bowl-shaped flowers open from late autumn into winter against glossy dark evergreen foliage, and the plant stays compact and shade-loving in cultivation compared with many sun-tolerant camellia hybrids. Grow it in filtered to deep shade in constantly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, since it comes from warm, humid limestone forest and resents both drought and hard freezes. Because it is markedly more cold-tender than Camellia japonica, gardeners outside mild coastal or subtropical climates grow it in a greenhouse or conservatory.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade with shelter from wind; Grantham's camellia is a rare Hong Kong forest species that benefits from protection against prolonged freezes.

directions: First described from Hong Kong Island in the 1950s and now critically endangered in the wild, with only a handful of native trees known on Hong Kong Island and Tai Mo Shan, Grantham's camellia bears some of the largest flowers in the genus: solitary white blooms four to five inches across with a dense central boss of golden stamens, opening in autumn and winter. Collectors grow it as a conservation-minded specimen shrub as much as an ornamental one, since propagated plants in cultivation help safeguard the species outside its tiny native range. Site it in partial shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil sheltered from drying wind, and expect slow, deliberate growth into a rounded evergreen shrub or small tree. It is somewhat hardier than fully tropical camellia species but still benefits from winter protection outside mild climates.
sources: Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, Hong Kong

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; fraterna camellia is among the more cold-hardy wild camellia species and tolerates more open sites than many tender tropical relatives.

directions: Native to hillside thickets and forest margins of east-central China (Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong), fraterna camellia is a compact, twiggy shrub valued by collectors for its small, single, white, intensely fragrant flowers opening in late winter to early spring ahead of most other camellias. It is noticeably more cold-tolerant than many showier wild camellia species, which has made it a favored parent in breeding programs aiming to combine fragrance and hardiness into hybrid camellias. Grow it in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, and allow it a somewhat more open, sunnier position than tender tropical camellia relatives would tolerate. Light pruning after flowering keeps the naturally twiggy habit tidy without sacrificing next season's flower buds.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade sheltered from wind; Pitard's camellia comes from mid-elevation forest in Yunnan, Guizhou, and Guangxi, China and resents both waterlogging and hot, exposed sites.

directions: Pitard's camellia grows wild in mid-elevation forests of Yunnan, Guizhou, and Guangxi in southwestern China, where its single to semi-double pink to rose flowers and broad glossy leaves closely resemble those of its better-known relative Camellia reticulata. Breeders at institutions such as the Kunming Botanical Institute have used it, and its variety yunnanica, as a parent of numerous large-flowered reticulata-type hybrids, but the straight wild species itself remains a sought-after collector's plant for its graceful, slightly looser flower form. Site it in dappled shade in reliably moist, acidic, well-drained soil with shelter from strong wind, since its broad leaves and large flowers bruise easily in exposed locations. Feed lightly after flowering and limit pruning to shaping, since flower buds form on the current season's new wood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; bladder-nut tolerates light frost once established but benefits from shelter while young.

directions: Bladder-nut is a slow-growing, dense evergreen shrub native to forest margins and rocky slopes of South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, grown widely in southern African gardens as a hedge, screen, or specimen for its small, glossy, dark green leaves and neat habit. Its most distinctive feature is the fruit: a small orange berry wrapped in a papery, salmon-pink to orange inflated calyx that persists on the plant and gives the shrub its common name. Like other Diospyros, it is dioecious, so both male and female plants are needed if ornamental fruit set is desired. Grow it in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants tolerate moderate drought and light frost, though young plants appreciate shelter.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Morris's persimmon is a frost-tender subtropical forest tree best suited to mild winter climates.

directions: Morris's persimmon is a wild evergreen ebony-family tree native to Taiwan, southern China, and northern Vietnam, grown by collectors of subtropical native trees for its glossy foliage and small, rounded orange fruit that ripen in autumn and are relished by birds. It is dioecious like other wild Diospyros species, so fruit set on a female tree requires a nearby male. In its native lowland and foothill forests it reaches moderate tree size, though garden specimens are typically kept smaller with occasional pruning. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and protect young trees from frost since the species is adapted to mild, humid subtropical winters.
sources: Flora of Taiwan, Taiwan Forestry Research Institute
